title: "Session 2 guided lab"
subtitle: "Set up course remotes and build a small Git history through RStudio"
---

::: {.callout-note}
**Suggested use:** complete the supervised setup checkpoint first. Checkpoints
1–6 then create three small commits through the RStudio Git interface. The
additional practice is a longer route that can be completed independently.
:::

## Goal

Use RStudio to clone the course repository, connect a private GitHub repository
through HTTPS, and review, stage, commit, and synchronize meaningful changes to
a synthetic-data analysis. Explain the repository state after every action.

## Setup checkpoint: clone, connect, and authenticate

Complete this checkpoint with the instructor or TA. The commands shown are a
supplied one-time recipe; you are not expected to memorize them.

::: {.callout-warning}
If you already have a course clone containing work, do not create another copy.
Open its root `BIOS6301-materials.Rproj` and begin with **Part B: inspect the
initial remote**.
:::

### Part A: clone the public course repository in RStudio

1. Select **File → New Project → Version Control → Git**.
2. Use this repository URL:

   ```text
   https://github.com/slzhao/BIOS6301-materials.git
   ```

3. Use `BIOS6301-mywork` as the **Project directory name**.
4. Choose the parent directory where you keep course projects.
5. Select **Create Project** and wait for RStudio to open it.

When the New Project Wizard appears, choose **Version Control**:

![](images/rstudio-new-project-wizard.png){fig-alt="RStudio New Project Wizard with Version Control as one of three project choices" width="76%"}

*Image source: [Posit RStudio User Guide](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/code/projects.html). The next screens ask you to choose Git and paste the repository URL.*

After cloning, confirm that the root project is open and that the **Git** tab is
visible. The exact filenames in your Git pane may differ from this example:

![](images/rstudio-vcs-pane-labeled.png){fig-alt="RStudio interface with the root project name, Git menu, and Git tab highlighted" width="88%"}

*Interface image source: [Posit RStudio User Guide](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/tools/version-control.html).*

### Part B: inspect the initial remote

Open RStudio's **Terminal** tab and run this read-only check:

```bash
git remote -v
```

Immediately after cloning, `origin` normally points to the instructor repository:

```text
origin  https://github.com/slzhao/BIOS6301-materials.git
```

This is expected. The next part preserves that address as `upstream` and assigns
`origin` to your empty private repository.

If `origin` already points to your private repository and `upstream` already
points to the instructor repository, do not repeat the setup commands. Continue
with **Part D**.

### Part C: connect the private `origin` and complete the first Push

Replace the username placeholder with your GitHub username. Use the plain HTTPS
URL without Markdown brackets, parentheses, or credentials:

```bash
git remote rename origin upstream
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/BIOS6301-mywork.git
git push -u origin main
```

The first private Push may open GitHub in a browser through Git Credential
Manager. Sign in, complete two-factor authentication, and authorize the helper
if requested. Then return to RStudio and read the Push result.

::: {.callout-note}
If you prepared **GitHub CLI** on macOS or Linux, run `gh auth login` before the
first Push. Choose **GitHub.com → HTTPS → Yes → Login with a web browser**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
If the Terminal requests your ordinary GitHub account password, cancel and ask
for help. Do not type a password or paste a personal access token.
:::

### Part D: verify the two-remotes arrangement

Run:

```bash
git remote -v
```

The addresses should have these roles:

```text
origin    your private BIOS6301-mywork repository
upstream  the public instructor BIOS6301-materials repository
```

Open your private repository on GitHub. Confirm that it now contains the course
files and commit history. This successful Push is the evidence that HTTPS
authentication works.

### Part E: verify course-staff access

In the private repository on GitHub, open **Settings → Collaborators**. Confirm
that invitations have been sent to:

- instructor: `slzhao`; and
- TA: `zongyue.teng@Vanderbilt.Edu`.

If either invitation is absent, select **Add people**, search for the account or
email address, and send the invitation. A **Pending** label is expected until
the recipient accepts. Keep the repository private.

![GitHub repository header with the Settings tab highlighted](images/github-repository-settings.png){width="100%"}

## Start the core lab from the repository root

1. Keep the root `BIOS6301-materials.Rproj` open.
2. Copy the complete `course/session02/starter/` folder to
   `work/session02-git-lab/`.
3. In the copied `analysis/` folder, choose `report.Rmd` or `report.qmd` and
   delete the unused alternative from the **copied work folder only**.
4. Do not initialize another Git repository or open a second project inside the
   copied folder.

The Git pane should now list the copied files as new or untracked.

## Checkpoint 1: Read the Git pane

Before staging anything:

1. Identify each copied file in the Git pane.
2. State why it appears.
3. Open `.gitignore` and identify which generated or local files it excludes.
4. Confirm that no credential, protected data, or unrelated file is listed.

Do not check every box until you understand every path.

## Checkpoint 2: Commit the analysis skeleton

1. Click **Commit** to open **Review Changes**.
2. Choose one copied file and inspect its diff.
3. Check the **Staged** box only after reviewing the file.
4. Repeat for `.gitignore`, `README.md`, your chosen `analysis/report.Rmd` or
   `analysis/report.qmd`, and `data/study_summary.csv`.
5. Switch between the **Staged** and **Unstaged** views. Confirm that staged
   snapshots exist for the intended four files—and no others.
6. Enter the message `Add reproducible analysis skeleton`.
7. Click **Commit** and read the result message.
8. Open **History** and locate the new commit.

Explain why this commit exists locally before it is pushed to GitHub.

## Checkpoint 3: Add a calculation

Open your chosen `work/session02-git-lab/analysis/report.Rmd` or `report.qmd` and
add a named object containing the mean outcome. Knit or Render and verify the
result.

Then use RStudio:

1. Return to the Git pane and refresh it.
2. Confirm that the chosen report source is listed as modified.
3. Confirm that the rendered HTML is absent because it is ignored.
4. Open **Diff** and identify the exact calculation added.
5. Stage only the chosen `.Rmd` or `.qmd` source.
6. Commit with the message `Calculate mean outcome`.
7. Verify that History now contains two lab commits.

## Checkpoint 4: Add an interpretation

Add one sentence that reports and interprets the calculated mean. Render and
check that the prose agrees with the calculation.

In **Review Changes**:

1. inspect the prose diff;
2. stage the source;
3. commit with `Add interpretation of mean outcome`; and
4. inspect all three lab commits in History.

## Checkpoint 5: Stage and unstage safely

Add this harmless temporary sentence to the copied `README.md`:

```text
Temporary staging practice.
```

1. Save and inspect the diff.
2. Check **Staged**.
3. Switch to the staged-diff view and confirm that its snapshot contains the
   sentence.
4. Uncheck **Staged**.
5. Confirm that the sentence remains in the working file.

This demonstrates that unchecking **Staged** stops preparing that snapshot for
the next commit; it does not change the working file.

After inspecting it again, use **Revert** to erase this known disposable edit.
Read the confirmation dialog before proceeding, and confirm that the file returns
to its committed state.

## Checkpoint 6: Push the recorded history

1. Confirm that the Git pane is empty.
2. Open History and reread the three messages.
3. Click **Push**.
4. The saved HTTPS credential should normally be reused. If GitHub opens again,
   complete sign-in and two-factor authentication there, then return to RStudio.
5. Read the result and confirm that the push succeeded.
6. Open your private GitHub repository and locate the three commits.

If the push is rejected, do not force push. Preserve the local work and ask the
instructor or TA to help identify which remote contains additional commits.

## Course update recipe

Run this only when the Git pane is clean and your own work is committed:

```bash
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
```

Interpret the lines rather than memorizing them:

1. Download new instructor commits from `upstream`.
2. Add those commits to the current branch.

Afterward, inspect the Git pane and the terminal result. If the update succeeds,
click **Push** so the updated history is also stored in your private `origin`.

## Additional practice: use the interface deliberately

1. Make one meaningful edit to your chosen report source and a different edit
   to `README.md`. In Review Changes, stage only the analysis, commit it, then
   commit the documentation separately. Explain why two commits are clearer
   than one.
2. Open History and compare each new commit with its parent. Identify the exact
   commit that introduced the analysis change.
3. Render the report again. Verify that the HTML remains on disk but absent from
   the Git pane. Explain the role of `.gitignore` without saying that it deletes
   anything.
4. Add a disposable line, stage it, unstage it, and verify the working edit
   remains. Then remove it by editing normally rather than using Revert.
5. Draw the three locations—working files, local commit history, and private
   GitHub `origin`—and label which RStudio action moves information between them.
6. Explain why RStudio **Pull** communicates with `origin` while the supplied
   course-update recipe communicates with `upstream`.
7. Examine this situation without performing any recovery: a file is modified,
   the Push button reports a rejection, and a classmate suggests force push.
   Write the safe next steps and explain why force push is inappropriate.

### Independent-practice check

Finish with an empty Git pane and a readable history. You should be able to show
which commit introduced each analytical idea, and you should be able to explain
why no command was needed for the everyday review–stage–commit cycle.

## Exit evidence

Show the instructor or TA:

- an empty RStudio Git pane;
- History containing the three core commits;
- the line-by-line diff for one chosen commit;
- a successful Push result; and
- `git remote -v` showing private `origin` and instructor `upstream`;
- the browser address of the private `BIOS6301-mywork` repository; and
- **Settings → Collaborators** showing invitations for the instructor and TA.

Explain the difference between a saved edit, a staged change, a local commit,
and a commit pushed to GitHub.
